Chapter 29

Hooks: identity, headers, one framed route, errors by kind

sequence of two handles, a preload filter that names font files by source filename, a per-route frame-ancestors swap, handleFetch, handleError that tells validation failures from real ones on the server and leaves a deliberate error(…) alone in the browser, init, the transport that carries an ErrorValue across the wire, and the two shapes of error a page has to read.

By the end of this chapter

Read every hook in the project and say what each is for — and what the September 2026 releases changed in them.

The types come from @sveltejs/kit/hooks, where SvelteKit 3 moved every one of them. The old import from @sveltejs/kit is now a type error — TS2305, “Module '"@sveltejs/kit"' has no exported member 'Handle'” — once for each name, followed by an implicit any for every argument those types used to describe, and pnpm run check fails on it. That was tried, in a copy of this project, rather than assumed. The one place an old import fails quietly is a hooks file written in JavaScript with JSDoc types and no checkJs, where nothing type-checks the file at all; in a strict TypeScript project like this one, it cannot slip through.

Three things in the security handle. The preload filter preloads the two font files the first paint needs, by source filename — in SvelteKit 3 a font input carries its filename, so nothing has to guess at a hashed URL. The security headers. And the one route that may be framed: the config says frame-ancestors 'none' for the whole app, and for /embed/ the hook replaces it after SvelteKit has built the policy. The config is the rule; the hook is the exception, stated once.

Why handleError looks at kind

SvelteKit 3 tells handleError what kind of error it is holding: app for a deliberate error(404, …), framework for its own, validation for a remote function argument that failed its schema, unknown for something genuinely broken. Only the last deserves a correlation id and a stack in the log; a validation failure logs the field path and answers with a plain message; the first two keep SvelteKit’s defaults. In SvelteKit 2 the hook never saw a deliberate error(…) at all and validation failures went to a separate handleValidationError; SvelteKit 3 sends every error here and kind says which is which.

init runs once, before the first request, and reaches the database. A deploy with a broken database becomes a process that never claims to be healthy — which is what a load balancer needs in order to keep the old version serving.

The universal hooks

SvelteKit serialises what crosses the boundary with devalue, which knows about Map, Set and Date and nothing about a class called ErrorValue. A transporter teaches it: encode returns a plain value for an instance (and something falsy for anything else, which is how devalue asks “is this yours?”), decode builds the instance back. A published sheet’s values arrive with real errors in them — instanceof works — rather than objects every consumer would have to rehydrate.

The client hook looks at kind as the server’s does. An error(404, 'No such template') thrown by a universal load while the browser is navigating arrives as app, and returning nothing keeps its status and message, so the error page says No such template and shows no reference — a 404 is not a bug. Only an unknown error, a component that threw, is logged and given one. In SvelteKit 2 the hook never saw an error(…) at all, so a hook that answered everything with “Something went wrong in this tab.” was harmless; SvelteKit 3 sends it every error, and the same five lines started hiding every deliberate message behind one sentence and putting a reference number on a missing page. The end-to-end suite now follows a link to a template that does not exist, and fails if that comes back.

Two shapes of error in the browser

Why a catch block and a failed snippet read different fields

Await a remote function in a handler — await publish(id), await form.submit(), await getPublished(id) outside the markup — and a refusal rejects with SvelteKit’s HttpError: { status, body }, where body is the App.Error the server’s hook produced. The sentence is body.message. It is not an Error, so (e as Error).message is undefined — an empty toast — and e instanceof Error ? e.message : 'Something went wrong' throws the server’s words away every time; this project had both. A boundary is the other shape. The SvelteKit docs say a failed snippet’s error “went through the handleError hook and is of type App.Error”: { status, message }, read as error.message. Neither was taken on trust. In a built app, a query that threw error(418, 'probe') reached a failed snippet as a plain { status: 418, message: 'probe' }, and a command that threw error(409, …) rejected its caller with an object whose own keys were status and body. In SvelteKit 2, sending render errors through handleError was an experimental option, handleRenderingErrors; in SvelteKit 3 it is how every boundary works, so the hook — not whatever was thrown — decides what a failed snippet shows. The module therefore has two functions, one per shape: messageOf for a catch, failureOf for a failed snippet, which Svelte hands an unknown and which reads the message after checking it is there, rather than with a cast that would compile whatever the shape.

Checkpoint

  • You can say what pnpm run check reports if the hook types are imported from @sveltejs/kit, and the one kind of project where that mistake would go unnoticed.
  • You can explain how /embed/ gets a different frame-ancestors from everything else.
  • You can list the four kinds and what each one gets from handleError, on the server and in the browser.
  • You can say what a catch around a remote call receives, what a failed snippet receives, and where the server’s sentence is in each.
